guided.title: First, last and length
guided.prompt: The variable `word` holds `"analytics"`. Print three lines: the first character, the last character (use a negative index), and the number of characters in the word. The expected output is `a`, then `s`, then `9`.
hints: Indexes start at 0, so the first character is at position 0.
A negative index counts from the end: `-1` is the last character. `len()` counts all characters.

guided.title: Cut a code into parts
guided.prompt: The variable `code` holds `"DF-2024-0137"`. Using slices, print three lines: the two-letter prefix, the four-digit year in the middle, and the last four characters (the serial number). The expected output is `DF`, `2024` and `0137`, each on its own line.
hints: A slice is written `code[start:stop]`; the start is included and the stop is not.
The prefix is `code[:2]` because a missing start means the beginning. The year starts after the first hyphen, at index 3.
The three slices are `code[:2]`, `code[3:7]` and `code[-4:]`; a missing stop means the end.

guided.title: Clean a name
guided.prompt: The variable `raw` holds `"  Ada LOVELACE  "`, with spaces at both ends and inconsistent capitals. Remove the extra spaces and convert the text to title case, then print it. The expected output is `Ada Lovelace`.
guided.solution:
raw = "  Ada LOVELACE  "
name = raw.strip().title()
print(name)
hints: String methods return new strings; they do not change the original.
`strip()` removes spaces from both ends and `title()` capitalises each word.
Chain the methods and print the result: `raw.strip().title()`.

guided.title: Check and replace
guided.prompt: The variable `email` holds `"sales@shop.com"`. Print two lines. The first is the answer to whether `"@"` appears in the email (`True` or `False`, produced by Python). The second is the email with `shop` replaced by `store`. The expected output is `True` and `sales@store.com`.
hints: The `in` operator gives `True` or `False` and can be passed straight to `print()`.
The `replace(old, new)` method returns a new string with every occurrence replaced.

independent.title: Mask an email address
independent.prompt:
The variable `email` holds `"maria.lopez@example.com"`. Without typing any part of the answers, print three lines. Line 1: the masked email, made of the first character, then `***`, then everything from the `@` onwards. Line 2: the domain, which is the part after the `@` (not including it). Line 3: the label `Local part length:` followed by the number of characters before the `@`. Use `find()` to locate the `@`. Expected output:

```text
m***@example.com
example.com
Local part length: 11
```
independent.solution:
email = "maria.lopez@example.com"
at = email.find("@")
print(email[0] + "***" + email[at:])
print(email[at + 1:])
print("Local part length:", at)

independent.title: Normalise a product code
independent.prompt:
The variable `raw` holds `"  Sku-4471-BLUE  "`. Clean it by removing the outer spaces and converting it to upper case, and store the result. Then print four lines: the cleaned code; the four-digit number in the middle, extracted with a slice; the colour (the part after the second hyphen) in title case; and whether the cleaned code starts with `SKU` (`True` or `False`, produced by Python). Expected output:

```text
SKU-4471-BLUE
4471
Blue
True
```
independent.solution:
raw = "  Sku-4471-BLUE  "
code = raw.strip().upper()
print(code)
print(code[4:8])
print(code[9:].title())
print(code.startswith("SKU"))

independent.title: Escapes and an underline
independent.prompt:
Print exactly the following five lines. The underline on line 2 must be created from the title with `*` and `len()` so that it is as long as the title. Line 3 contains backslashes. Line 4 contains double quotes. Lines 5 and 6 below must come from a single `print()` call that uses `\n`. Expected output:

```text
Monthly Sales
=============
File: C:\data\sales.csv
Status: "ok"
Rows: 120
Errors: 0
```
independent.solution:
title = "Monthly Sales"
print(title)
print("=" * len(title))
print("File: C:\\data\\sales.csv")
print("Status: \"ok\"")
print("Rows: 120\nErrors: 0")
independent.expected:
Monthly Sales
=============
File: C:\data\sales.csv
Status: "ok"
Rows: 120
Errors: 0

checks.question:
What does this program print?

```python
word = "python"
print(word[1:4])
```
checks.explanation: The slice starts at index 1 (`y`) and stops before index 4, so it holds the characters at indexes 1, 2 and 3: `yth`. `ytho` would include the stop index, and `pyth` or `pyt` start counting at 1 instead of 0.

checks.question:
What does this program print?

```python
name = "ada"
name.upper()
print(name)
```
checks.explanation: Strings are immutable, so `upper()` returns a new string and leaves `name` unchanged. The new string was never stored, so `name` is still `ada`. You would need `name = name.upper()` to keep the change. The call itself is valid, so there is no error.

checks.question:
What does this program print?

```python
print("ab" * 3 + "c")
```
checks.explanation: `*` repeats the string three times and is worked out before `+`, giving `ababab`, and `+` then joins `c` to it. The repeat applies only to `"ab"`, not to the whole expression, so `abcabcabc` is wrong.

checks.question:
What does this program print?

```python
print("data" in "Database")
```
checks.explanation: The `in` test is case-sensitive. The text `Database` contains `Data` with a capital D, but not `data`, so the answer is `False`. The result of `in` is always `True` or `False`, never a position.

checks.question:
What does this program print?

```python
print(len("a\nb"))
```
checks.explanation: The escape sequence `\n` stands for one single character, the newline, so the text has three characters: `a`, newline and `b`. Counting the backslash and the letter n separately would give 4.

checks.question:
What does this program print?

```python
text = "banana"
print(text.find("x"), text.find("n"))
```
checks.explanation: `find` returns the index of the first match, or `-1` when the text is missing. The first `n` in `banana` is at index 2 (counting from 0), not 3, and the missing `x` gives -1, not `None` and not 0.
